claims.text: Ethanol oxidation involves a full 12-electron and 12-proton transfer process.
The catalyst's performance is governed by dynamic formation of a surface Pt-oxide/hydroxide interface.
The Pt-oxide/hydroxide interface tunes the binding energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The interfacial oxide/hydroxide layer facilitates proton-coupled electron-transfer steps.
The interfacial oxide/hydroxide layer retards structural degradation of the catalyst.
Changing the applied electrochemical potential modulates the extent of oxide/hydroxide formation on Pt.
An optimal Pt oxide layer changes the electronic properties of the catalyst.
Electronic changes caused by the optimal oxide layer modulate intermediate binding energies and facilitate PCET.
Oxide-mediated modulation of binding and PCET produces superior catalytic activity and selectivity.
The optimal oxide layer enhances durability by mitigating over-oxidation and structural degradation.
Potentials favoring optimal Pt-oxide/hydroxide formation will produce high ethanol-oxidation current densities.
Potentials favoring optimal Pt-oxide/hydroxide formation will improve selectivity for complete ethanol oxidation.
Potentials favoring optimal Pt-oxide/hydroxide formation will extend operational durability.
Suppressing oxide formation or causing excessive oxidation will reduce activity and selectivity.
Suppressing oxide formation or causing excessive oxidation will accelerate catalyst degradation.
Prior reports indicated high activity and durability at moderate applied potentials.
The proposed mechanism applies under controlled aqueous ethanol-oxidation conditions at ordinary pH and temperature ranges.
The proposed mechanism may fail at very high temperatures, in non-aqueous media, or at potentials causing irreversible catalyst damage.
